ai.definition: Nuclear fusion is a process in which atomic nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing vast amounts of energy. In a fusion reactor, this process mimics the conditions inside stars like the sun, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium under extreme temperatures and pressures.
ai.howItWorks: Fusion reactors heat plasma (ionized gas) to temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius using various techniques such as magnetic confinement or inertial confinement. The high temperature causes deuterium and tritium isotopes of hydrogen to undergo fusion, producing helium and releasing energy in the form of neutrons and gamma radiation.
ai.problemSolved: Fusion power addresses the global challenge of providing a sustainable, low-carbon source of energy that could replace fossil fuels. It promises virtually unlimited fuel supply from seawater and minimal waste with short-lived radioactive byproducts.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing fusion reactors involves complex engineering challenges such as developing materials resistant to extreme temperatures and radiation, designing efficient magnetic confinement systems or laser-based inertial fusion systems, and integrating advanced control systems.
ai.buildProcess: The build process begins with selecting a reactor design (tokamak, stellarator, laser-fusion), followed by detailed engineering, component fabrication, assembly, testing, and commissioning. Each step requires specialized equipment and expertise.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the high initial capital investment for research and development, advanced materials, complex manufacturing processes, and long-term operational costs for maintaining reactor integrity and safety systems.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Despite decades of research, fusion power remains in the experimental phase with no commercial reactors yet built. Current projects aim to demonstrate net energy gain within the next decade, but widespread deployment is not expected before mid-century or later.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for fusion power are still evolving. Existing nuclear regulations may apply, requiring stringent safety standards and environmental impact assessments. Specific regulations will depend on national policies and international agreements.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving net energy gain, developing materials that can withstand extreme conditions, and ensuring reactor safety. Economic risks involve the high cost of R&D and potential delays in commercialization. Environmental risks are minimal due to low-level radioactive waste from deuterium-tritium fusion.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the current state of research and lack of commercial-scale deployment. Break-even points for fusion power plants could be decades away, depending on technological advancements and policy support.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on improving reactor designs, reducing costs through economies of scale, advancing materials science, and addressing safety concerns. International collaboration is likely to accelerate progress in this field.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of megawatts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and high-temperature operations.

glossary.def: A stable isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron, used as a fuel in fusion reactors.
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons, also used as a fusion fuel. It can be produced from lithium-6 through neutron capture.
An ionized gas composed of free electrons and ions, often used in fusion reactors to contain the reaction.
A toroidal-shaped device that uses magnetic fields to confine plasma for nuclear fusion reactions. It is one of the leading designs for practical fusion power generation.
Another type of fusion reactor design that uses a complex, non-circular magnetic field configuration to confine plasma without an external current drive.
